Placental imaging showed a normal-appearing placenta for twin 1 and a thickened, echogenic placenta for twin 2. These findings prompted suspicion for twin anemia-polycythemia sequence and an emergency cesarean section at 32 + 2 weeks.

vignette:
A 47‐year‐old woman presented with crescendo chest pain, palpitations, and shortness of breath on exertion for two days. In the emergency department she was hypotensive, tachycardic, and tachypneic. Physical examination showed bilateral fine basal crepitations, a grade 2 decrescendo diastolic murmur, and bilateral pitting lower‐limb edema. She was an active smoker working in warehouse logistics, with no history of substance misuse or family history of cardiovascular disease.

Chest radiography demonstrated congested basal lung fields with mild bilateral pleural effusions. Electrocardiography showed ST-segment depressions in the inferior leads. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed anterior‐wall hypokinesia and moderate‐to‐severe aortic insufficiency; immobile echogenic shadows in the ascending aorta obscured the aortic valve. A computed tomography aortogram excluded aortic dissection. Urgent coronary angiography via the radial approach showed a slit-like left main coronary ostium while the remainder of the coronary arteries was free of atherosclerotic plaque.

These atypical findings prompted investigations for infectious and inflammatory aortitis. Potential causative organisms under consideration included Treponema pallidum, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Salmonella species, Staphylococcus species, and Campylobacter jejuni. Musculoskeletal examination and immunological assays were not suggestive of rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, or Behçet disease.

vignette:
A 55-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and opioid use disorder presented with worsening abdominal distention and a 60-lb unintentional weight loss over 1 year, along with increasing difficulty with bowel movements. He denied melena, nausea, vomiting, fevers, flank pain, dysphagia, or odynophagia, and had no history of abdominal surgery.

Three weeks before admission, abdominal CT with contrast showed a small-bowel obstruction with a transition point in the right-mid abdomen and focal small-bowel wall thickening, plus mesenteric adenopathy. His symptoms improved without intervention, and he was discharged.

He returned 3 weeks later with diffuse abdominal pain. Repeat CT showed multiple dilated loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels. Colonoscopy revealed two polyps; cold-forceps biopsies showed non-specific chronic inflammation without features of inflammatory bowel disease. Video capsule endoscopy demonstrated erythematous gastritis, multiple small-bowel ulcers, and an atrophic duodenum. Two weeks later, double-balloon enteroscopy identified multiple jejunal strictures and areas suggestive of inflammatory bowel disease, and outpatient IBD management was planned.

Two months later, he presented with severe abdominal pain, new nausea, and vomiting. Abdominal radiographs suggested pneumoperitoneum. Exploratory laparotomy revealed a perforated ulcer in the terminal ileum, which was repaired, and a proximal Brooke ileostomy was created. Biopsies around the perforation showed ulcerated mucosa with non-specific chronic inflammation. He was discharged after a 21-day hospital stay.

One month later, he was re-hospitalized for non-specific abdominal symptoms and increased ostomy output. Ileoscopy showed scalloped mucosa with blunted villi throughout the ileum, and biopsies were taken. Histologic examination revealed extensive lymphocytic infiltrates with epitheliotropism but no definitive atypical morphological features, raising suspicion for a lymphoid neoplasm. A hematopathology consultation was obtained.

An 8-year-old girl weighing 44.5 kg with no significant medical history presented with a 1-week history of progressive abdominal pain, distension, nausea, and vomiting. Physical examination revealed notable abdominal distension without guarding or rebound. Initial abdominal ultrasonography showed a 17 × 9 cm mixed solid and cystic mass occupying the right hepatic lobe with compression of the inferior vena cava (IVC). By hospital day 7, worsening abdominal distension and concern for abdominal compartment syndrome prompted percutaneous biopsy of the mass and placement of a drain. Over the next several days, persistent sanguineous output from the drain led to anemia and concern for hemorrhage. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated an infrarenal IVC thrombus and a near-occlusive embolus in the left pulmonary artery. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed compression of the distal IVC at its junction with the right atrium, with otherwise normal biventricular function and no evidence of elevated right heart pressures.

vignette:
A 67-year-old man was referred for further evaluation of icterus and upper abdominal pain. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a diffusely enlarged, sausage-shaped pancreas with delayed enhancement and a capsule-like rim, together with intrahepatic bile-duct dilation. FDG-PET showed diffuse uptake in the pancreas (SUVmax 8.6) and multiple hypermetabolic lymph nodes (SUVmax 10.0). vignette:
A 25-year-old woman, gravida 3, presented to the gynecology clinic with 6 weeks of amenorrhea, right lower–quadrant abdominal pain, and vaginal bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasonography showed an empty uterine cavity and a gestational sac in the right adnexa without fetal cardiac activity. The serum β-hCG level was 585 mIU/mL. She received intramuscular methotrexate (50 mg/m2) on day 1, with a decline in β-hCG to 19.1 mIU/mL on day 4 and 9.8 mIU/mL on day 7; because of persistent low levels, a second dose of methotrexate was administered.  

Shortly thereafter, she noted pain and swelling in both knees. On examination, she was afebrile and appeared well. Both knees were diffusely swollen and tender to palpation. Laboratory tests revealed a hemoglobin concentration of 12 g/dL, a white-cell count of 13,600/L, and a platelet count of 576,000/L. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 100 mm/h, and the C-reactive protein level was 43 mg/L. A plain radiograph of both knees was unremarkable. Joint ultrasonography revealed anterior soft-tissue swelling with a thickened synovium and fluid collections measuring 1.0×0.9×2 cm in the right knee and 1.1×0.9×1.8 cm in the left.

vignette:
A 34-year-old North African woman with no significant past medical history was referred for management of obstructive jaundice. Two months earlier, she had undergone laparotomy and resection of the protruding dome of a segment I hepatic cyst thought to be a hydatid cyst compressing the biliary convergence. She now presented with fever to 38.5 °C, mucocutaneous jaundice, dark urine, and pale stools. On examination, she was febrile and icteric; there was no abdominal tenderness, hepatomegaly, or palpable mass. Laboratory studies showed moderate hepatocellular enzyme elevations and cholestasis. Hydatid serology and serum carcinoembryonic antigen and carbohydrate antigen levels were negative. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed a cystic lesion in segment I with parietal and septal enhancement and rupture into the biliary convergence. MRI demonstrated a multiloculated lesion that was hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2, communicating with the biliary bifurcation, with dilatation of intrahepatic ducts (predominantly left) and of the common bile duct containing heterogeneous signal material. At laparotomy via a subcostal incision, the liver appeared micronodular; on opening the common bile duct, mucinous fluid and membranes were extracted, raising questions about the presumed diagnosis.

vignette:
An 83-year-old man presented with 6 months of progressive right mandibular pain radiating to the zygomatic and mastoid regions, requiring oxycodone, paracetamol, and ketorolac for relief. An empirical course of prednisone (50 mg per day) for presumed trigeminal neuralgia provided no benefit. Contrast-enhanced maxillofacial CT showed enlargement of the right sphenoid sinus with overdevelopment and opacity of the lateral recess, bone thickening and sclerosis of the sphenoid walls, pterygoid process, and orbital apex, and focal interruption of the foramen rotundum and lateral recess wall. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI demonstrated soft tissue protruding through a breach in the lateral recess wall of the sphenoid sinus, invading the right internal pterygoid muscles, masticatory and pterygopalatine fossae, and infiltrating the V2 and V3 trigeminal branches; intracranial extension into the cavernous sinus surrounded the Gasserian ganglion, with the cavernous carotid artery patent. T2-weighted images showed a markedly hypointense signal in the lateral recess with peripheral mucosal inflammation. Endoscopic evaluation revealed purulent discharge in the sphenoethmoidal recess. The patient underwent right endoscopic sinus surgery: after middle turbinectomy, the sphenoid ostium was obstructed by a pyocele, which was marsupialized and drained; samples of the lesion and surrounding mucosa were sent for bacteriological and histopathological examination. The maxillary and ethmoid sinuses were then opened, the breach in the posterior-lateral sphenoid wall was repaired with mucoperiosteum, and a Merocel sponge was placed. He was discharged after 2 days without complications. Histopathology was negative for hyphae and neoplastic cells, and cultures grew no bacteria or fungi. One month after surgery, follow-up MRI confirmed persistent inflammation of the sphenoid sinus, skull base, and pterygoid fossa. A consultation with an infectious diseases specialist was sought.

vignette:
A 35-year-old man presented for routine follow‐up 11 years after a left total hip arthroplasty with a ceramic‐on‐ceramic articulation. Over the preceding 3 months, he had left buttock and greater trochanteric pain, initially attributed to overuse. He denied fevers or systemic symptoms. On examination, range of motion of the left hip was full and painless; there was focal tenderness over the posterior buttock and greater trochanter but no palpable mass. Anteroposterior radiographs of the pelvis and left hip were unchanged compared with images obtained 1 year earlier. A diagnosis of greater trochanteric bursitis was made, and an intra‐bursal corticosteroid injection was administered, resulting in partial symptom relief.

Six weeks later, he returned with persistent buttock pain and intermittent electric shock–like sensations radiating down the left leg. Physical examination now revealed decreased and painful range of motion of the left hip with continued tenderness over the greater trochanter. A lumbar spine radiograph was normal. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 22 mm/h (reference range, 2–28), a C‐reactive protein level of 14.4 mg/L (reference, <10.0), and an alkaline phosphatase level of 318 IU/L (reference, 40–125). Hip aspiration yielded 10,750 white cells/μL; all cultures were negative. Serum cobalt and chromium levels were within normal limits. A metal artifact reduction sequence MRI revealed a left periprosthetic soft‐tissue mass measuring 9 × 8 × 10 cm, without bony involvement or bone‐marrow edema.

vignette:
A 56-year-old African American woman with no significant past medical history presented with a six-day history of progressive swelling of the left labia, which ruptured and began draining serosanguinous fluid two days before admission. On arrival, her temperature was 36.8 °C, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg despite intravenous fluid resuscitation, pulse 96‒100 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 17.4 × 10^9/L. Empiric intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam were initiated, and a surgical consultation was obtained. Pelvic CT imaging demonstrated an ulceration of the left labia with air in the subcutaneous fat of the left groin and lower abdominal wall, as well as inflammatory fat stranding along the left lateral abdominal wall. The Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis (LRINEC) score was calculated as 3, with the potential to rise to 7 pending C-reactive protein results. Despite non-definitive laboratory and imaging findings, concerns for sepsis, subcutaneous gas on CT, and the LRINEC score led to the decision to proceed with immediate exploratory surgery.

vignette:
A 74-year-old man with a history of interstitial pneumonia presented with one month of right-sided chest pain that worsened with inspiration and severe sweating confined to his right arm and thoracic area, accompanied by a cold sensation. He denied abnormal sensation or muscle weakness. Six months earlier, chest CT had shown dense infiltrates in the ventral subpleural regions of the right upper and middle lobes; on admission these shadows had enlarged. Oral antibiotic therapy failed to improve the infiltrates, and he was admitted for further evaluation.

On examination, he was sweating profusely on the right arm and right thorax. Vital signs were blood pressure 150/78 mmHg, pulse 71/min, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. A pleural friction rub was heard over the right chest. The skin on the right arm, chest, and back was moister and cooler than the left. Thermography revealed decreased surface temperature over the right arm and right thorax corresponding to dermatomes C5–T12. Pupils were equal and reactive; eyelids were not droopy. Neurological examination showed no sensory deficits or abnormal reflexes.

He had no history of smoking, trauma, or asbestos exposure. His medical history included hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and varicose veins, treated with candesartan and ezetimibe. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 9,000/μL and C-reactive protein of 1.14 mg/dL. Intravenous antibiotics were started on admission, but his symptoms, inflammatory markers, and imaging findings did not improve. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage revealed macrophages 65.1%, lymphocytes 4.8%, neutrophils 29.9%, and eosinophils 0.2%, with no microorganisms or malignant cells. A transbronchial lung biopsy showed no malignancy or specific inflammation.

vignette:
A 51-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of gradually progressive pain and swelling below his left knee, accompanied by intermittent fevers. Three months before presentation, the swelling ulcerated. He remained ambulatory without assistance.  
On examination, there was a firm mass measuring 30 × 18 × 12 cm over the distal tibia extending into the calf, with an anterior discharging ulcer 12 cm in diameter and areas of necrosis. The discharge was yellow and thick. Knee range of motion was reduced, and there was tenderness over the left knee and proximal tibia. Distal pulses (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial, popliteal) were intact and lower-limb neurologic examination was normal. Other systemic examination findings were unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. Chest radiograph showed no abnormalities. Plain radiographs of the left leg demonstrated a large metadiaphyseal lesion of the tibia with soft-tissue opacity, bone erosion and destruction of the tibia and adjacent fibula, and linear and ring-like calcifications, with extension into the proximal leg soft tissues. A Tc-99m bone scan revealed increased tracer uptake in the shaft of the left tibia and proximal soft tissue, without evidence of distant skeletal metastases. MRI was not obtained due to financial constraints.  
Based on the clinical presentation and radiographic appearance, the leading considerations were osteosarcoma and chondrosarcoma of the tibia. On admission, the patient received intravenous antibiotics and analgesics and was counseled regarding treatment options. Taking into account lesion size, secondary infection, prosthesis cost, and prognosis, the patient elected transfemoral amputation with plans for postoperative chemotherapy.

A 62-year-old woman presented with 4 months of soreness, swelling, and limited movement of her right palm and wrist. Six months earlier, she had been stabbed by a fishbone. She had been diagnosed with a tenosynovial giant cell tumor by MRI at a local hospital and treated with traditional Chinese medicine, but her symptoms worsened over the past 2 months. She denied respiratory symptoms, skin disorders, recent travel, or tuberculosis exposure and had no family history of inflammatory arthritis or psoriasis. On examination, there was swelling, tenderness, and limited motion of the right palm and fingers without percussion pain or bone friction. Physiological reflexes were intact. Laboratory studies showed normal leukocyte count, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate; rheumatoid factor was negative. Noncontrast MRI of the right hand demonstrated patchy abnormal signal around the deep flexor tendons and carpal canal, with hypointense signals on T1-weighted imaging and hyperintense signals on proton-density fat-suppressed sequences. Post-contrast images demonstrated homogeneous enhancement of the tendons and synovial membrane, supporting synovial hyperplasia, while diffusion-weighted imaging and ADC maps suggested restricted diffusion. The median nerve was mildly compressed and deformed, and degenerative changes were noted in some carpal bones. Ultrasonography showed rough, thickened bone surfaces and decreased echogenicity at the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints and along multiple flexor tendons, with peripheral and internal flow on color Doppler. The flexor retinaculum was elevated, and the median nerve was flattened at the carpal canal. Based on these findings, preliminary diagnoses included degenerative arthritis, synovitis, tenosynovitis, and atypical carpal tunnel syndrome; a neoplastic lesion remained in the differential.

vignette:
A 9-year-old boy was referred with left cheek swelling and hyperglobus of the left eye. Hyperglobus was first noted about 1 year earlier under ophthalmologic observation. Six months later, swelling of the left cheek developed, with marked progression over the preceding 3 months. 

On extraoral examination, there was a painless, bony-hard swelling of the left cheek. The overlying skin was normal, but the patient reported numbness of the left cheek and weakness in movement of the left upper lip. There were no other neurologic deficits, no visual disturbances, and ocular motility was intact. Intraoral examination revealed expansion of the left maxillary ridge with mobility of primary teeth c, d, and e.

A panoramic radiograph and cone-beam computed tomography demonstrated a large, well-circumscribed, expansile, heterogeneous (mixed-density) mass occupying the entire left maxillary sinus. The lesion caused deviation and destruction of the nasal septum, invaded the ethmoid sinus, thinned, displaced, and perforated the anterior wall of the sphenoid sinus, extended into the pterygopalatine fossa with destruction of the pterygoid plates, and elevated and perforated the left infraorbital rim. There was extreme postero-superior displacement of the second molar toward the inferior orbital fissure, resulting in blockage of the fissure, and compromise of the nasopharyngeal space.

Medical history was notable for seasonal allergic reactions and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency; blood pressure was documented as 10/5 mmHg. Coagulation studies were within normal limits. Laboratory evaluation showed WBC 19 × 10³/μl, RBC 3.66 × 10⁶/μl, hemoglobin 10.6 g/dl, hematocrit 33.2%, and MCHC 31.9 g/dl; other serum chemistries were normal.

An intraoral incisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia with mepivacaine to minimize the risk of methemoglobinemia.

vignette:
A 72-year-old man with a history of stage IIIA gastric cancer treated by distal gastrectomy and adjuvant S-1 six months previously developed peritoneal and para-aortic lymph-node recurrence treated with weekly paclitaxel. After seven courses of chemotherapy, he experienced progressive anorexia and general fatigue and was referred for further evaluation.

On admission, he was alert. Temperature was 38.5 °C, blood pressure 110/53 mmHg, heart rate 64 beats/min, weight 60.2 kg (BMI 22.3 kg/m2). He had no skin or mucosal hyperpigmentation and normal pubic and axillary hair. Chest and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory tests showed: WBC 1.97×103/µL with neutrophils 350/µL, hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL, platelets 199×103/µL; CRP 3.1 mg/dL; blood glucose 101 mg/dL; electrolytes on admission normal (Na 141 mEq/L, K 4.1 mEq/L, Cl 101 mEq/L). He was treated for febrile neutropenia with G-CSF: his neutrophil count and fever improved within three days, but his anorexia and fatigue worsened, rendering him bedridden. One week after admission, his ECOG performance status declined from 2 to 4. On hospital day 5, laboratory tests revealed Na 122 mEq/L, serum osmolality 239 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 482 mOsm/kg. Fluid intake was restricted to 1 L/day for presumed SIADH, but the hyponatremia persisted.

Gonioscopy demonstrated open angles bilaterally with diffuse trabecular hyperpigmentation in the right eye. Anterior-segment OCT revealed increased reflectance of the iris surface in the right eye. Standard automated perimetry detected early visual-field defects in the right eye, and peripapillary OCT showed borderline retinal nerve-fibre-layer thickness on the right. Topical latanoprost was initiated in the right eye, reducing intraocular pressure to 17 mm Hg.

vignette:
A 34-year-old Filipino man presented with a 4-month history of left eye proptosis, diplopia, and chemosis without epistaxis, headache, or nasal obstruction. Endoscopic nasal examination revealed a mass at the level of the left middle turbinate extending into the left nasal roof and eroding the upper nasal septum. Ophthalmologic evaluation showed mild left proptosis with full extraocular movements, no papilledema, and normal visual acuity. Contrast-enhanced CT of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated an expansile, mildly enhancing soft-tissue mass in the anterosuperior nasal cavity encroaching on the left orbital cavity, with remodeling of the left medial orbital wall and extension to the level of the cribriform plate, along with retention of secretions in the left frontal sinus. MRI (T1-weighted postcontrast) showed an enhancing mass reaching the nasal vault without dural enhancement or intracranial extension; T2 and non–contrast T1 sequences revealed no intratumoral hemorrhage or cystic change. The patient underwent endoscopic endonasal resection, which disclosed a cystic mass occupying the left fronto-ethmoid region with destruction of the anterior skull base and erosion of the left lamina papyracea; the dura was exposed but intact, and no cerebrospinal fluid leak was noted. A routine functional endoscopic sinus surgery was completed after tumor excision.

vignette:
A 5-month-old dark-skinned boy was seen for evaluation of a congenital skin lesion on the left supraclavicular area. At birth, the lesion measured 11 cm × 3.5 cm; at 5 months it measured 10 cm × 2.5 cm. On examination, it was a single, nonpulsatile, well-demarcated, dark brown atrophic plaque with a linear midline depression and an elevated, compressible, soft border that was paler than the central portion. Birth and neonatal history were unremarkable; the patient was healthy and not on medications. The initial differential diagnosis included smooth muscle hamartoma, semiannular lipoatrophy, and, less likely, a rapidly involuting congenital hemangioma (RICH). A small vein (~0.3 mm) was visible to the naked eye within the plaque. To avoid puncturing larger vessels during a planned biopsy, an AccuVein AV400 infrared vein finder was used; it revealed one large vein with an extensive network of small superficial branching vessels localized to the area of the atrophic plaque. A working diagnosis of probable RICH was made.

A 33-year-old Hispanic man with no known past medical history presented with a 1½-week history of headache and blurred vision. MRI of the brain demonstrated a 2.7-cm ring-enhancing lesion in the right temporal lobe with mass effect. He underwent craniotomy with biopsy and resection. CT scan of the chest confirmed extensive reticulonodular interstitial infiltrates with focal consolidation in the left upper lobe. He was started on vancomycin, piperacillin/tazobactam, and fluconazole and placed on airborne precautions.
